utterances.text: The age references are contained in the reports of the pathologist, in this case Dr. John Clark.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning then to the issue of cause of death, Mr. Manning, can you indicate what were the findings largely, in brief?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: In brief, the cause of death was normally defined as multiple gun shot wounds or gun shot wounds. A significant proportion of the individuals were identified as -- that was a cause of death. Other causes of death were gun shot wound and blast injury, or blast injury alone. A significant proportion of the individuals were determined to have died of causes -- unspecified causes -- undetermined causes, sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Then going back to Exhibit 549/107. Can you indicate just briefly what is the significance of this photograph as to the nature of the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This photograph shows not only the robbing process in the grave, but if you see the individuals, particularly the one at the top of the grave, the skeleton there, his arms are in a posture. Many of the individuals have their arms in that posture because they were ligatured, they were tied, and there was evidence located at Kozluk mass grave, indicating the victims had been shot in situ. That is, bullet wounds to the skull and body and corresponding bullets below the bodies. The majority of the individuals in this photograph have their arms tied behind their backs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there -- was there any grave site where the cause of death was determined as being different from the other graves?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: There was some difference as to percentage, but the cause of death in the majority of cases was gun shot wound and/or blast injury. And in some cases there were indications that cause of death were unknown. There were small numbers of blunt force trauma indicated. But in all, gun shot injury was the cause of death, the main cause of death.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in which grave or graves were the blast injuries found?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Specifically they were found within the Glogova 1 and 2 graves. Also, the Branjevo Military Farm graves, and the corresponding secondary grave, particularly Zeleni Jadar 5 and 6, evidence of blast injuries were found. Although that was difficult to ascertain in the graves due to the breaking up of the bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at page 2 of your report, Exhibit 554, in relation to the 2001 findings, you noted down the breakdown of the number of persons who died of various injuries such as gun shot wounds. Those numbers do not appear to match with the MNI or the MMNI that we saw earlier. Can you explain that.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Effectively, it's the same problem as I detailed before with the bodies being broken up. The cause of death indicated in the reports is a sign where it's possible if you have an individual who is -- his skull is missing, perhaps, and there are no visible injuries to the rest of his body, you can't assign a cause of death. However the skull might have a bullet wound to the skull, or the skull might found without the rest of the body with a large bullet hole in it indicating the cause of death of that individual's gun shot injury. If you add all those figures up you get more than the MMNI or the MNI. I think that represents a representation of the large number of bodies represented by these body pars, but also indicates on occasion the example I used where you have a skull which has a clear cause of death and you have a body without a skull with a clear cause of death, that body -- those two body parts can be counted twice as cause of death.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, using the map, can you just give us a brief overview, Mr. Manning, of some of the methods used to link the primary and secondary graves. I know you mentioned it earlier, but if you can just verbally tell us what those methods were.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I said, perhaps the Kozluk is a good indication. We found bottle labels and thousands and thousands of pieces of broken green glass. In fact the Kozluk execution point, a large number of the bodies were killed on fields of broken green glass and bottle labels, which corresponded to a bottle factory which was approximately one and a half kilometres away in the town of Kozluk, or near the town of Kozluk. Those bottle labels and thousands of pieces of broken glass were transported to the secondary grave and were located amongst the bodies in that grave. Also located in the secondary graves that was exhumed, Cancari road 3, were the same bottle labels with the address of the bottle factory. Also used in linking the graves was a soil and pollen analysis. Dr. Tony Brown examined the soil from the grave, from the secondary grave. Using his expertise in relation to the pollen present, the type of soil, the granular part of the soil, the microfossils, et cetera, he established that the soil type at Kozluk was significantly different to the area of Cancari road. However the soil in the Cancari 3 grave was significantly different and it matched that at Kozluk. Therefore, the soil had been taken along with the bodies and the broken glass and the bottle labels from Kozluk to Cancari road 3. Similarly, the shell cases that were located in and amongst the bodies in the grave, the Kozluk grave, were transported when the grave was robbed and placed in Cancari 3. We collected those shell cases and a large number was sent to the American Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms lab where they examined the ejector marks on those shell cases. Those ejector marks are formed when the shell case is thrown from the weapon, and they are individual to that weapon, microscopically. They were able to match the shell cases from the Kozluk primary grave with those in the Cancari 3 primary grave, showing that the shell casings were fired by the same weapon. Similarly, blindfolds and cloth ligatures were collected from both sites. They were examined by the Dutch Forensic Institute. Dr. Susie Meljaz [phoen] examined those blindfolds and grouped them into blindfolds and cloth ligatures which were significantly the same. She continued her investigation and identified those blindfolds and cloth ligatures which were indistinguishable from each other. And thence provided a link from the primary grave, type of blindfold used, to the secondary grave, type of blindfold and cloth ligature used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, dealing then with the blindfolds and ligatures, aside from using them to link the primary and secondary graves, is there any significance to locating the ligatures in general?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Well, clearly the individuals that were blindfolded and ligatured, and some were blindfolded and ligatured, were executed. A cause of death would be fairly clear, that they were murdered. In many instances we found blindfolds in situ on the skull with a corresponding bullet wound to the skull and a corresponding hole to the blindfold, which indicated that they had been shot through the blindfold through the head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. How many blindfolds in total were found in the various mass graves?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I examined all the cloth blindfolds, and I made a conservative count of them, which is 448. However, I did eliminate quite a number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you say it's a conservative count?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I examined not only the autopsy and exhumation records and the photographs and the body sheets and the various documents, but also I physically finished the artifacts. And I tried to be very conservative and only produce a blindfold or a ligature as an exhibit which I could categorically prove had been either on a skull very closely associated to a body, had perhaps human hair on it or a bullet wound corresponding to a wound on the skull, or where that documentary and photographic path was complete, if there was a blindfold identified at the grave site but because of the transportation of the body or the examination or the simple errors that can occur in such a massive process, that chain of custody was lost, I didn't count that item or artifact. If it was described as a possible blindfold or a possible ligature and I couldn't corroborate that, then I would discount it. I also discounted the large number of cloth blindfolds collected at the Grbavci school and also near the Orahovac mass graves in 1996. I had not been part of that process, and there had been collected and a representative sample taken, so I ignored those blindfolds. I believe 219.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning then to Exhibit 650 which is a chart that's entitled "Blindfolds and Ligatures Located 1996 to 2001." Looking at the bottom of the chart with respect to blindfolds, can you very briefly explain the different exhumation sites where the blindfolds and the cloth material was located.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: If you look at this table, it indicates the number of blindfolds that were located, the graves that it was located in, and the -- where the blindfolds were located, either the head or the face, closely associated with the body or loose in the grave. That is, not directly associated with the body and the various totals for that. Similarly on the top of the table, ligatures are described in the same manner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to indicate the sites where blindfolds were found in terms -- in the sense of making a distinction between the primary and the secondary graves?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, the primary grave of Branjevo Military Farm, two blindfolds were located. The Orahovac 1 mass grave site, which is a primary site, 138 were found. Orahovac 2, which again is a primary site, 107 were found. At the Orahovac 2C, which is connected to 2, 40 blindfolds were found, and that's again a primary site. And at the Kozluk primary site, 55 were located. And at the Glogova 1 primary mass grave, 3 possible blindfolds were located.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why are they listed as possible?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: They were packing tape, plastic packing tape, which the chief archaeologist described as either a blindfold or perhaps a gag. They were around the eyes, but they had deteriorated to such a point and particularly as they were exhumed that they started to fall apart before analysed, if you like. Therefore, we couldn't conclusively conclude that they were blindfolds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning next to Exhibit 560, can you indicate what this -- I think that's the wrong exhibit on the screen. If we can refer to another exhibit, Exhibit 547/96.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is a photograph taken at the Visoko mortuary. It represents an individual who was designated as body 41 from the Lazete Orahovac 2 grave which was exhumed in 1996. You can see the individual has a cloth blindfold which stretches across his eyes. It is one of the blindfolds that has a specific pattern which was reoccurring across quite a number of the graves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain how these photographs came into existence and what ultimately happens with the items that were found on the bodies?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is an initial photograph on receipt at the mortuary of the body. The body was then examined by the pathologist. The blindfold and other artifacts are removed, the clothing is removed and cleaned. The pathologist then examines the body and he then takes the clothing which has been cleaned and examines it with the body in an attempt to identify evidence such as bullet wounds through the blindfold or clothing. The artefacts such as this blindfold are then processed by the scene of crime officers and then ultimately processed through the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning then to Exhibit 557, which I believe is on the easel there, collage, can you explain what this exhibit represents.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a collage of all the blindfolds that were located amongst the Srebrenica-related graves. I prepared this in grave order, if you like. So the Branjevo Military Farm is first. Its related secondary grave of Cancari 12 is next and so on and so on. It represents a single photograph of each blindfold; there are no duplications. And one thing it indicates is the striking similarity between some types of blindfolds and some types of blindfolds across the various graves, including the matched primaries but also the other primaries and secondaries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Each grave is listed there with the different blindfolds following depicted. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's correct. As I say, the primary grave is first, such as Orahovac, Lazete 2, and then the secondary graves connected to that grave such as Hodzici 3, 4, and Hodzici 5. And the primary grave of Kozluk, the related secondary grave of Cancari road 3. And last is the three, described as "possible blindfolds" from Glogova.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Perhaps with the assistance of Madam Usher we can refer to Exhibit 558.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. Manning, that there were some ligatures found in the mass graves. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Total number of the ligatures that were found.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: 423 ligatures were located amongst the mass graves. And again, on the table I present the numbers where they were located. And this is a similar collage showing again the ligatures, exactly the same format. The primary grave, the related secondary grave. It represents a single photograph of the ligatures, although I believe if you look at the Glogova 1 ligatures, in this case two men were ligatured together. They were both tied and then they were both tied to each other in pairs. So that represents each of those pairs and the ligatures that bind them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And Your Honours, Exhibits 545 through 548 and 550 contain the individual images that are depicted in this collage as well as the previous one we saw of all the blindfolds and ligatures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Manning, the figure of 423, is that a conservative or a liberal figure?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Again, I used the same methodology that I used to provide an accurate count of the blindfolds. Some ligatures were not sufficiently described or photographed, and I excluded them. Where ligatures were made of the same material as blindfolds, it was quite clear because of the construction, the width of the circles and the number of circles, that they were a ligature rather than a blindfold. But when they were broken to the point that I couldn't tell that, then I would exclude them as either a blindfold or a ligature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Referring back to Exhibit 650, the chart of the blindfolds and ligatures, can you just take us very briefly through the top portion of the chart entitled "ligatures." How many were found in the various primary and secondary grave sites.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Again, the primary grave are listed. Cerska, 48 individuals were found to be bound; Nova Kasaba 1996, 27 individuals; Orahovac 1 or Zeleni 1, there was four individuals; Orahovac 2 was one individual, again they are primary graves; Branjevo Military Farm, 83 ligatures were located; the primary grave of Petkovci dam, one was located; at the grave at Kozluk, 168 ligatures were located; and at the Glogova 1, as I have previously explained, 12 sets of ligatures were located, double ligatures if you like, and that was a primary grave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you elaborate on that, the 12 sets of ligatures that were located. When you say there were 12 sets, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That grave was designated as grave L. I was present when that grave was located and exhumed. And what we found was that an individual had been tied at the wrist by a string ligature. Another individual had been tied at the wrist by a string ligature and those two ligatures were then tied together. So you had two adult males tied together. That continued, so there were six sets of adults tied together in pairs. And the subsequent autopsy of those bodies or the initial examination of those bodies, I was present at the Visoko mortuary. And in each of those cases, the individuals had been shot in the head. Some had been shot again in the body. And we found some shell cases and some bullet -- bullets within the grave, indicating that they had been shot in situ. That was also supported by the posture of the individuals who had seemed to have fallen into the grave as they were tied together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning then to Exhibit 550/186, can you indicate what that represents.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is a photograph at the Visoko mortuary, and it represents two bodies or two arms -- sets of arms of the bodies. On the left is the body designated as 301 and you can see that the ligatures go around the two bones of each forearm. Then that ligature extends across to two bones of one forearm of the other individual, body 302. In this image, they simply haven't placed the other set of arms because they had come loose from the binding. But this represents the two individuals that were bound and then bound together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning then to Exhibit 550/183.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is grave L. And the reason why that photograph we saw previously was shown is that it's very difficult to see in these graves what's actually happening. But if you look at the first individual, his head is pointing to the right of the photo and his arms are in that familiar posture, that they're bound behind his back. If you look to the left top of the photograph, you can see another set of arms running up to an elbow in a shirt; that's the other individual who was behind him. And there was evidence of some other string ligature surrounding their wrists where they were joined. And as indicated, the skull is fractured badly in this individual. And as I said, I saw the autopsy, which indicated that they had been shot in the head. This grave was a long, thin grave, and this process of twins tied together and killed or dead in a grave progressed up the length of the grave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Manning, you mentioned in describing grave L, which was a particular subgrave of Glogova, that these individuals were tied with a string ligature. Were there other types of material used as ligature in the various graves?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes. There were three main types of ligature used, although some types of material was opportunistically used such as a cloth sack. But in some graves such as this one, string ligatures were used. Twine. Also, wire was used, such as in Cerska. And in Nova Kasaba 96 where all the ligatures were of fencing wire. And as I indicated before, ligatures were made of cloth, similar material to some of the blindfolds, individuals were bound by cloth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning then to Exhibit 545/114, can you indicate what this photograph represents and coming from which grave.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Again, this is a photo at the mortuary at Visoko, and it is a cloth ligature. It is showing the arm of one individual designated as body 719. You can see that the ligature had wrapped around his wrist more than once, and the other circle that's visible was wrapped around the other arm, which in this instance is not visible. This was quite usual to see, cloth ligatures used in this figure of 8, and that's one reason I was able to ascertain if they were loose whether they were a ligature or a blindfold.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is coming from which grave?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: From the Kozluk grave, the one on the Drina river with the green glass.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning then to Exhibit 549/087 what does this photograph indicate?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is the Nova Kasaba 1996 mass grave, which was exhumed in 1996 clearly, hence the flesh condition of the body. This is behind the man's back, you can see his wrists crossed over, and very, very tightly bound by wire ligature which extends past the number there. And as I said, all the ligatures in Nova Kasaba 1996 were of wire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In dealing -- moving on then to another area, and that is the area of identification, I'm going to be asking you about two categories of identification. Firstly, we'll be dealing with the identification of a place where the victims came from. And secondly, we'll be dealing with what led to the identity of the victims themselves. Can you first of all tell us, Mr. Manning, whether the victims in those graves were identified as having come from a particular place.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes. In almost every single grave we found some form of identification or some indication that the individuals in the grave were from Srebrenica. And indeed, one of the processes that we did when we first exhumed a body was to effectively try and prove that they weren't from Srebrenica. We were conscious that we didn't always -- we weren't always sure that we found the grave connected to Srebrenica. So we would go through the belongings, we would search through the identification materials, until we found something that indicated a connection to Srebrenica, be it an identification book, an inscribed artefact or an identification document which matched an individual reported as missing from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you -- have the artefacts linked to Srebrenica been located in all the primary mass graves or the secondary mass graves?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: All the graves that I speak of have been linked to Srebrenica, but not all of the graves identification material has been identified. I believe in the case of Konjevic Polje 2, which is a small mass grave, no identification material was found. But the creation date matched Srebrenica. But in the case of the other graves, some material was located, which indicated a connection to Srebrenica. Such connections were not only identifications, but Dutch newspapers, Dutch medicine, Dutch medical reports, all connected with the DutchBat base at Srebrenica were all connected to the -- before July of 1995, such as Dutch newspapers from the month before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning then to some of the exhibits that illustrate these types of artefacts, Exhibit 549/095. Can you indicate, Mr. Manning, what this photograph depicts.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a necklace with a medallion on it. This was located in the Cerska mass grave which was exhumed in 1996. This artefact was found in 1996 and led to the identification of an individual who was identified as Cerska 60. The families of the missing from Srebrenica were called upon by the organisation Physicians for Human Rights and the Red Cross to make reports in relation to the missing, in relation to the dead. Part of that was to describe the belongings of the victims, describe things that would help in the identification process. One woman was able to make a drawing of a pendant which she had given her son, and she described that pendant; she drew a picture of it. And she also indicated that it had been knotted, a knot had been placed in the chain. He was a young male, I think 16 years of age and the pendant was too long. So she saw him knot it and place it around his neck. That pendant, as you see here with the S on it and the knot, was located on the body. That was shown eventually to the family, and she was able to immediately identify that artefact that she had given to her son. And as a result, further examination, such as the examination of ante- and post-mortem data established that the individual Cerska 60 was indeed her son. And that identification came about because of this family gift.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning then to Exhibit 549/095A, can you identify what this document is.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is a page from the ICRC/PHR missing list. I believe this is the version produced by the ICTY, and it shows a BAS [phoen] number which is a number assigned to a missing person, the name of the missing person, the gender, date and place of birth, and disappearance. And this indicates the individual who was identified, highlighted here as Elizabet Selimovic, his date of birth, from Srebrenica, and missing in the year of the -- this is what the document or type of document we used when we located identifications. We sought to match those to lists of missings -- missing people and confirm the identity of those individuals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning then to Exhibit 549/093, what does this photograph depict?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is actually an artificial leg which was removed from a body in the Pilica or Branjevo Military Farm grave in 1996. It was taken from a body. The significance of this artefact is that the tape that you see binding the leg, repairing the leg is marked Unis Feros Srebrenica and Yugoslavia. It's a type of packing tape which I am familiar with. And I believe that the Unis Feros factory is located in or near Potocari, again a clear indication that this individual had a connection to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning then to Exhibit 549/093A, what is the significance of this document?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Again, this is a missing persons' list. The fact that there was an official leg on an individual significantly lowers the range of who he might be amongst the missing persons. So the artificial leg not only provided a link to Srebrenica, but it provided assistance in identifying that individual who was wearing that artificial leg as this individual.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning then to Exhibit 656, what does this photograph depict?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is a watch found in the secondary grave of Zeleni Jadar 6. Again, that's the grave or one of the graves connected to Glogova and hence the warehouse. It was located in the grave, not connected to a body. And it has an inscription which includes the words "Unis Feros" Srebrenica and the year 1985 [sic]. Again, that's the Unis Feros that's indicated on the packing tape from the leg and a clear indication that this individual is connected to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning then to Exhibit 657. What does this photograph depict?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is a good example of the type of identifications we found later on in the exhumation process. It has deteriorated quite a significant amount. But if you see in the top left-hand side, you can see the word "Srebrenica." Often when we removed these documents from the grave they would fade as they were exposed to the oxygen and the light. In examining, we saw that this was connected to Srebrenica, and has the name of an individual, his date of birth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning then to Exhibit 658. What is the significance of this document?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Again, the list of the missing from Srebrenica, and it indicates the individual who was identified from that identification booklet as listed as missing following the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And who is that?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Dahmo Kadric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, half-way down the page.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: It's, if you like, bears 912181/2, Dahmo Kadric, a male. His date of birth is not indicated in full in this version of the document; however the year of birth is clearly indicated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the name -- that same name on the wallet or in the photograph we saw previously?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, when you examine that identification booklet, it has that name on it and the date of birth, complete date of birth of Dahmo Kadric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning then to the issue of religion, or faith, in the course of exhumations, Mr. Manning, can you tell us whether there were any artefacts that indicated what faith the victims belonged to.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, in almost all the graves we located clear evidence with an affiliation of the Muslim faith, which included copies of the Koran, Koranic texts, prayer beads. And in fact, we found nothing which would indicate a different religious affinity. We either found no artefacts or we found artefacts which indicated an Islamic or Muslim connection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning then to Exhibit 549/110. By way of example, what does this photograph depict?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is a photograph of an artefact located on -- in the Hodzici secondary grave, connected to the Orahovac primary graves. It is taken at the mortuary and it shows on the bottom right-hand -- a packet which contained the Islamic verses on the left. This was a reasonably good example of what we would find. We would also find lockets with miniature Korans or parts of the Koran in them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving on then to the issue of the photographs found in the graves, can you tell the Chamber whether there were any photos found during the course of exhumations and where, if so, where?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: We found a significant amount of photographs mainly in the wallets of the individuals or loose in the graves. Many of those photographs were the standard photographs that you or I would carry, the wives, children, significant people. In the early days, those photographs were able to be recovered quite easily. As the exhumations continued, a number of those items were deteriorating, but we did manage to collect quite a number of photographs and documents from the wallets or pockets or possessions of the individuals. These photographs include, as I say, photographs of what I assume to be family members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the significance of finding the photographs among the individuals?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: In a similar way to the chain, the medallion, they were able to help us identify, or try to identify the individuals located within the graves. Attempts were made to show those artefacts to family members. And books were produced in Bosnia of artefacts and clothing which had been located, distributed amongst the surviving families and widows in an attempt to identify the bodies. If an artefact was identified, then that would lead to an examination which would hopefully lead to an identification.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning then to Exhibit 549/001, can you indicate what this photograph depicts?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is a photograph located in the Lazete 2 Orahovac 2 primary mass grave. It's one of at least 12 items located on body 36. And it's, as I say, a family photograph. It's just one of the photographs, the many photographs, in this instance that we found which we would hope to be able to use to identify the victims. I just indicate on that photograph where there's a date on the top right-hand corner in red 5/9/96. That was the mortuary photograph. That's not part of the photograph found in that grave. So that's a later addition from the exhumations of taking a photograph of a photograph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there any effect to removing the bodies from the primary and secondary graves on the -- on physical evidence such as photographs?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: As I said, the disruption to the bodies was quite massive, including the loss of these sort of artefacts. They were either torn from the bodies or they were exposed to the soil and the air and the water, et cetera. But also you would find a set of legs with an identification in the pocket. But you wouldn't be able to match that to the rest of the body, so it made it much more difficult.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Manning, the Court has heard that documents and belongings were actually taken from the men during their detention. In relation to the number of bodies in graves, how many such documents did you find?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me to say. We found a significant number, but we didn't find many significant belongings such as backpacks or bags or belongings. These were things that were held in pockets or in coat pockets. I would have to examine in excess of 10.000 exhibit reports to indicate how many specific items such as this were located.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning then to Exhibit 549/006, can you indicate what this depicts and what its significance is.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Again, this is a photograph from body 236 at Orahovac primary grave; it's item 12. Again, it's a photograph of a child. This set of photographs were bound together by this tape, and this is the same Unis Feros tape that you see on the artificial tape. And again, not only is it hopefully showing a family member that could be a source of identification, but it links this individual again to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning then to Exhibit 549/018. Can you indicate what that depicts and the significance, please.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Exactly the same. It's from a different grave and it indicates, unfortunately, the deterioration of the photos that happens. This is from body 11 at Branjevo Military Farm. It shows a normal family gathering. We tried to preserve this material as much as we could because we hoped to use it for identification.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And has this photograph led to the identification of an individual?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it has.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning then to Exhibit 549/018A, are you able to tell us, looking at that document, which is the IC -- a page from the ICRC list, who that individual was?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, I believe from the examination conducted that the body was identified as Elizabet Selimovic with a date of birth of the 3rd of January, 1962.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that a male or female?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's a male.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it might be an appropriate time to take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, it's time for a break and we'll resume at 12.30

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Issa.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Manning, just for a few more points that I would like to go over with you. You mentioned earlier grave L, the 12 bodies that were tied together by twos. I'm not sure whether or not you recall this, but do you have any information as to when the grave -- when grave L was created by virtue of the aerial imagery that you reviewed earlier?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Professor Richard Wright, in exhuming that grave, along with the rest of Glogova 1, examined the aerial imagery. And in his report he indicated that that grave had to be created after the other graves -- well, the majority of the other graves. Without checking his report, I believe it was after the 17th of July there was a window of creation time that had to be after the 17th up until -- and I can't recall the dates at the moment. I apologise. But it was certainly created after the 17th, perhaps 19th or 20th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned -- just dealing with the linking of the primary and secondary graves, you've given us a very good overview in the manner in which these graves were linked. Just very briefly referring to Exhibit -- sorry, I've lost my page -- 556. Can you just identify that very briefly for us. We're not going to go into it in detail since you've done this already.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a table I created, basically a different representation of the map. It just highlights along the top the primary mass graves, or in the case of the warehouse, the Kravica warehouse, the execution point, the related primary grave in that case. And then the related secondary graves flowing on from that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in dealing with the shell casing, you mentioned that some of the primary graves were connected to secondary graves via shell casing. Just by way of example, turning then to Exhibit 559, can you indicate what that depicts.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness make a pause of 2 seconds before answering.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My apologies. This is a photograph of a body at Kozluk mass grave. I recognise it to be body 501. It's a blindfolded and ligatured body, and you can see the green glass that I spoke of before, even though it's a black and white image. But of interest in this photograph is in the centre, perhaps down to the right, is a shell case located next to that body. When this body was exhumed, that shell case was located there and it's an example of the shell cases that we located amongst the bodies and amongst the graves, which were then examined by the ATF in America.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And you've indicated that the shell casings were in fact used to link primary and secondary graves. Was there a report submitted by the bureau of alcohol and tobacco firearms?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes. By experts, including Mr. Martin Ols of that bureau.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that report is at Exhibit 562. You reviewed this report, Mr. Manning?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I reviewed the result of that report. I also had detailed conversations with Mr. Ols and other members of the ATF in relation to the examination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you very briefly describe the findings in the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may interrupt. This material came in through 92 bis. Now, the reason it came in is because we didn't challenge or we weren't challenging at the time. However, now it appears they're trying to give some validation to that report through this gentleman, who I assumed was coming here to testify about the burial process and what he did. Now he's being used as a summary witness to resummarise the entire Prosecution's case. I do object to him commenting about the reports unless he generated those particular reports, otherwise we can read the reports, the Court can draw its own conclusions from the reports. There is no need to waste time with this gentleman going over material that was introduced through 92 bis at the behest of the Prosecution. If they wanted to do a long, delayed process of bringing in all the individuals and getting all those reports in through the individuals, they could have brought them. Instead, they chose another way. Now they're trying to revisit all those reports and all those experts through this gentleman. And if they didn't want to go through the front door, Your Honour, they shouldn't be trying to get through the back door or through the basement window at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Ms. Issa?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I am not going through all the reports. The reason I'm referring to this report specifically is because this was one of the reports that actually was not put in through the 92 bis or 94 bis pursuant to that ruling that I referred to earlier and we are seeking to tender it. So I wanted to very briefly give it a bit of context. And as I recall Your Honour's ruling, the Prosecution was permitted to have Mr. Manning testify about this report and seek to tender it through Mr. Manning. And I can find the passage in the ruling for Your Honour, if you would like me to, but that's the reason I'm referring specifically to this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: As I said, they didn't want to go through the front door; now they're trying to go through the back door. They could have easily asked to have this come in through 92 bis. In all likelihood, because I'm rather familiar with this sort of forensic evidence as opposed to what we were dealing with yesterday, demographics, I probably would not have objected. But now I do object to using this gentleman here who is not a forensics expert. He's certainly not a ballistician. We're discussing this based on hearsay that he heard from their expert. So I think if they are trying to lay a foundation, I guess I'll wait, I'll listen, and at some point, I probably will object because it wasn't brought in through the avenues in which they should have brought it in initially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Issa, on this issue, I agree with the Defence counsel. You cannot introduce a report written by somebody else through this witness. And in your question, it's very general. Unless you find something specifically related to the question you asked previously. So please, if you want to continue, please ask a specific question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour. Perhaps I'll just move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And if need be, I can return to the point -- I may not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving then on, sir, to Exhibit 648.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honour, while we're trying to find that exhibit we can move on to another area to save time, and if need be we can return to that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated, Mr. Manning, that a number of graves were actually linked via the shell casing comparisons. Did -- was there a time when they actually tested guns from the Bratunac Brigade or weapons linking them to a particular grave site? Did that ever occur, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was involved in a major part of that process in which weapons were seized from the Bratunac Brigade, the Zvornik Brigade, and other brigades or units in the area of Srebrenica. Those weapons were test fired and shell cases were collected with the intention of comparing shell cases to the shell cases located within the graves. That was conducted by Mr. Ols and his associates. I do not recall the ultimate outcome, but I understand it was unsuccessful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Just then turning back to Exhibit 648 very briefly. Can you indicate, sir, exactly what that chart is, just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I produced this chart following my examination of the ATF report. And on the basis of that report, I indicated which graves had been linked via that shell case examination, the Kravica warehouse, Zeleni Jadar 5, Cerska 2, parts of the Cerska grave itself, the Lazete to the Hodzici secondary graves, the dam -- to part of the dam and Kozluk, primary grave to Cancari road 3. The significance of perhaps linking the Cerska grave to the Cerska surface roadway and north side of the road was that there was an indication that the execution had happened at the side of the grave. This was comparing the shell cases located within the grave to those where we believe the executionists had stood, and those shell cases matched.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you indicate, Mr. Manning, what you're relying upon in providing that analysis or those results that those shell casings matched?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, from examining Mr. Ols's report he indicated laboratory numbers. They didn't mean anything to the investigations team, so we -- I examined the laboratory numbers, matched them to the artefacts that we had sent them and then produced this table of the results of that examination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at this point, Mr. Manning, are you able to briefly describe the findings of that report or elaborate on what you've indicated earlier in relation to matching -- the way in which the shell casings were matched?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I think I indicated before that the examination consisted of a microscopic examination of the ejector marks which are found on the shell case where the weapon flings the shell case out. It strikes it with a piece of metal, marks it. Each microscopically-examined mark should be the same from same weapon. This would indicate that if a shell case was found at a primary grave and a secondary grave, either the shell cases were moved from the primary to the secondary or the weapon that fired both shell cases was at both locations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, given that we've already discussed the other links, blindfolds, ligatures, soil comparisons, and the green glass, I don't propose to go over that again. Now, I notice on the map you do have a link at the very -- at the southern-most point of the map between Glogova and Zeleni Jadar as being linked through artefacts. Can you describe the nature of the -- this artefact connection just to remind us.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I said, there were a significant amount of artefacts located in the Glogova graves, the primary graves, which were identical to those in the Kravica warehouse. Those artefacts were seen at the Zeleni Jadar 5 grave but very strongly at the Zeleni Jadar 6 grave. I was present for a significant part of that exhumation, and we found pieces of the building structure itself, pieces of metal, pieces of what we call a fin, a decorative part of the warehouse, including layers of paint and foam insulation material from the wall of the warehouse. Those materials were found in the Zeleni Jadar 6 grave. They matched those significantly found in Glogova 1 and 2 and they matched those still present at the warehouse. So we based that connection predominantly on artefacts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was any evidence collected at the site aside -- leaving aside the artefacts, was there any other evidence collected at the Kravica warehouse?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes. The -- apart from artefacts which we used to compare from the primary grave and the secondary graves, the Pilica -- sorry, the Kravica warehouse was examined by the U.S. Naval criminal investigations service in 1996. And suspected human blood and human tissue samples were taken along with suspected explosive residue samples.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning then to Exhibit 10.11. While we're trying to find the exhibit, Mr. Manning, can you describe how the blood samples were collected, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I would indicate that this is from the examination of the reports by the U.S. Naval investigation service. I wasn't present. They were obtained by simply scraping the residue from surface, from the walls and the floor and placed into appropriate paper containers, sealed and processed. That was for the collection of the blood and residue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, in addition to the blood and residue, was there any other material collected or observed at the warehouse that indicated it was a crime scene?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes. There was significant indications of blood and human tissue, hair located on the walls, on the ceiling, on the floor of the warehouse which is still present and still visible to a very large degree. Also located was clear evidence of burning and scorching, explosive residue patterns, and again samples were taken by the U.S. Naval investigation service. Also located at that time were fragments of skull, bone, human bone, ammunition, and other artefacts. In subsequent examinations, part of which I was present for, grenade fly-off levers were located outside the warehouse adjacent to the windows at the rear of the warehouse. There was also an examination of a through and through hole through the rear wall of the warehouse and the reinforcing concrete had been forced out in that location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the significance of that?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: One of the survivors of that execution had indicated the use of a rocket-propelled grenade. Examination of that hole was consistent with such a weapon being used, and parts of the rocket-propelled grenade were located amongst the bodies in the Glogova grave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you -- did you attend at the warehouse along with the experts?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I didn't attend in 1996; however, on numerous occasions, particularly whilst exhuming the Glogova, Ravnice, and Zeleni Jadar graves, I attended the warehouse with police and scientific officers as well as photographers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were the dimensions of this warehouse?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: The warehouse is actually a collection, a long collection, of several buildings separated by a small room in the middle, if you like. The major examination was conducted on the eastern end of the warehouse. I've indicated that it's about the size of this courtroom, perhaps a third wider, with a 45-degree angle sloping roof, very large door on the eastern end, windows along the sides, and another doorway to the western end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning then to Exhibit Number 10.3, can you very briefly identify what that photograph depicts, please.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is the Kravica warehouse. It's taken in winter. It is the eastern end to the right of the photograph with a large damaged doorway. And the other doorway which I mentioned is the one to the middle left of the photograph next to the four open areas. I'd indicate that I spoke before of the foam lettering above the door, which was located at the Ravnice grave. That's that little doorway with the lettering above it. The other part of the warehouse was not significantly examined by myself or the other teams.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Turning then to Exhibit 10.4 -- or rather, 10.11. Just very briefly, Mr. Manning, what does that photograph depict?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This photograph I recognise to be a still from a short video section of a film known as the Petrovic video. It is taken as a car travels from the east to the west along the road, and that's the large doorway that you see in the warehouse. In this image, the doorway is not yet damaged. I strongly believe that they are bodies of those executed in the warehouse. And in the audio section of this tape, you can hear gunfire. And on the right-hand section you can see a male person. In the video you can see that he's armed. You can see pock marks on the wall which are known to be impacts from weapons, rifle fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning next to Exhibit 10.4. Can you indicate, Mr. Manning, what this photograph depicts.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is a section of the wall of the warehouse. I spoke about the windows at the rear of the warehouse, below which we found a number of levers from grenades. This is looking towards the back wall. It shows the window. It shows some of the blood and what looks to be explosive residue patterns on the wall. I would indicate that there is significant burning within the warehouse. Our examination showed that at some stage prior to the execution, burning had occurred, but also during the execution some burning had occurred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The next crime scene that you indicated earlier was examined was the Pilica Dom. Can you just very briefly indicate what -- how was it examined, what was collected at the Pilica Dom.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Again, the Pilica Dom is an execution point. I've indicated that it's the top of the map near the Branjevo Military Farm. It's a community building. It was examined in 1996 by the U.S. Naval investigation service, the same people who examined the Kravica warehouse. And again, they took representative samples of blood, human tissue, and explosive residue from that building. They also identified large amounts of blood and explosive damage to the stage, blood dripping from the stage, artefacts such as shell cases, identification documents, and shoes, and other material which indicated or confirmed that an execution had taken place in that building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning then to Exhibit 19.7. Can you indicate what that photograph depicts.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is a photograph of the stairway area leading to the stage of the Pilica Dom. There is a blood splatter pattern. You can see it's dripping down the wall, and there's another pattern on the left of the photograph. And it also indicates damage to the walls and the structure of the Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dealing with the explosive residue or the damage to these two structures, can you indicate whether or not there was an analysis produced by any of the experts.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, following the collection of those artefacts and those samples, I conveyed them to the Netherlands Forensic Institute where they were examined by experts at the constitute. They concluded that one of the samples of explosive residue found at the Pilica Dom contained traces of the high explosive TNT and two traces of explosive residue located at the Kravica warehouse contained similar traces of high explosive TNT.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And the report that you're referring to was for the record Exhibit 655.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: And I have no further questions. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much. I think you are ahead of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Cross-examination, Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just have a few questions. Cross-examined by Mr. Karnavas:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning or good afternoon, Mr. Manning.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From looking at your CV, it appears that up until 2002 you were working at -- in various capacities, primarily with the exhumations of the bodies and collection of evidence and working with those experts. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, my main duties were, as described, however I was also involved in statement taking and interviews and similar investigative work. But all focused on the Srebrenica case for team 6.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. My question was: Up until 2002. Because from your CV, it looks as if at that point you became the team leader for this investigative process. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's not correct. In 2000 -- September 2002, I became team leader of a separate team, team 4, involved in the investigation of offenses in Croatia and not connected to the Srebrenica investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So you would have been the one, I take it, determining who would be interviewed, when they would be interviewed, by whom they would be interviewed, since you were the team leader of this investigative process from the moment you started working with OTP?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, just to clarify the point, whilst from 1998 to September 2002 I was a team member of team 6 investigating Srebrenica, under the command of two separate team leaders. I then left that team and became a team leader of a completely separate team. So I did not direct the activities of the Srebrenica team, except on occasion when I performed acting team leader duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And that was for a brief period of time, four months. Is that what you state here, 2001?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I performed those duties for a four-month period continuous, and over the years as a member of team 6, I performed those duties as needed for various periods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the answer is yes?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, four months plus whatever other occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Was that prior or after the arrest of Colonel Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I was in team 6 on the arrest of Mr. Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So while you were working on the Srebrenica team, as I see from the interviews of the various witnesses, it appears that you're present quite often and in fact quite often you're rather engaging in asking questions. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: During the time that I was on team 6, I interviewed a large number of witnesses and I also interviewed a number of suspects. You're correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, is there any reason why you never made any efforts, you or your team, to contact Mr. Blagojevic who was in the RS, in Banja Luka, at the time working openly with the international community. Is there any reason why you never made any efforts to see whether he would be willing to give a statement to you or other members of the OTP, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm trying to pause to assist the interpreters, but I would have to check the records. But I would have assumed that an attempt was made to speak to Mr. Blagojevic. I don't recall making that attempt. That's a question I can't answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But if you say that you could check your records, could you please do that and if you find anything where attempts were made by you or others to actually go to Banja Luka on your various trips to locate him where he was working openly with the international communities, could you please give us that information. Because we haven't found it so far and I have been on this case for -- almost the time he was arrested. Okay?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps that a request best dealt with by the team, but I would be happy to assist. I know that we interviewed other suspects, other accused who were eventually brought here. Because I'm no longer associated with the team, perhaps it's best that request was made of the team.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That is a request that has never been made to me and I'm in one of the best positions to answer that. I would certainly be able to answer that to Mr. Karnavas should he ask, and I can actually provide the Court with that information as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me be very clear on this point, Your Honour, let me be exceedingly clear on this point. This has been a point of contention throughout an eight-month period when I filed numerous motions well over ten motions with respect to Mr. Blagojevic's provisional release. And this issue has been asked repeatedly over and over and over again. There have been a lot of innuendo that they had to uncover his whereabouts. But pressed, and I invite the Trial Chamber to look at all of my motions and all of my insistence for the Prosecution to produce a scintilla of evidence where efforts were made to contact Colonel Blagojevic, especially after I point out to him that when they interview General Zivanovic who was the commander up until the 12th or 13th or 14th of July of the Drina Corps, and Zivanovic says Blagojevic is a good man and you ought to talk to him and we have McCloskey say, Yes, that's a good idea. In spite of all of that, there's actually no evidence to show that he was ever contacted or any evidence that efforts were ever made to contact him. And since this gentleman was a team leader or was working in that capacity as an investigator, and I note that he does this by profession, I was just curious whether he could provide us with that information, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I believe that you could ask a question to this witness, and we also believe that the witness has already answered that question. The other matters are the matters between you and the Prosecution. I hope after this session the two of you will meet together to clarify this issue. If there is still some problems which are related to this case, you may or both parties may freely come to the help of the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I just have a couple of other questions. You went through a series of photographs, aerial photographs, that were provided to you, I take it, by the United States government, aerial photographs. And using those photographs, you were able to determine disturbances on the ground and those assisted you in finding the burial sites or some of the burial sites. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I take it that when you made that request it was for a specific period of time, probably from the 10th or 11th of July, maybe even earlier, until August or September, October, or the end of 1995. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, we made numerous requests for this material over various time periods. I would agree with you that we requested specific periods and then we would get what was available or what was released to us. In the case of the Orahovac grave, we were looking for a -- the earliest -- sorry, the latest time when it hadn't been disturbed and the earliest time when it had been disturbed. So within those ranges, we would make requests.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Could you please tell us, if you know, the sort of -- the first date that you were looking for, you know. Was it July 6th when we believe the attack on Srebrenica occurred, or was it, say, after July 11th when we know that most of the folks have gone to Potocari and some have gone -- are on their way towards Tuzla. Can you give us an indication, if you know, what was the first date of the request.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I didn't make those early requests particularly for the primary graves that were located by the time I had joined the team. And I am somewhat hesitant because I am aware that some of those procedures are covered by Rule 70. But in the case of Orahovac where we have a survivor who indicates when the grave was created, the requests were made, and again I didn't make them, with the intention of saying: Can you provide an image that shows the closest time to the creation date of that grave. So was it created before Srebrenica happened? Was it created the minute it happened? Those requests were made in line with the testimony of the survivor. The images that were provided were provided by the U.S. under their control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now -- and I don't want to get into any Rule 70 material, but I take it that for each burial site you were -- you tried -- I'm only -- I'm making an assumption now. I don't know. You tried to get some assistance from the U.S. government to provide you with some photographs at or around that period when witnesses were telling you that incidents were occurring. Is that a fair assumption?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So for instance, we know that -- and I think this is with some certainty, with respect to the Kravica warehouse, that that incident happened on the 13th of July. We don't know the exact hour or minute when all things began, but at least we have that particular date. Would you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I accept that the Kravica warehouse massacre occurred on the 13th of July in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, did you make a request for the 13th of July then to see whether the aerial imagery would be able to assist us in pinpointing the time, for instance, you know when a mass of people were there entering into the warehouse or gathering around the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Again, Your Honours, I didn't make those requests, but there are aerial images that show the warehouse on the 13th in the afternoon. One that I know of, it shows a bus at the western end of the warehouse. That I believe to be significant because it corroborates a witness testimony of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And would the aerial imagery tell you the time, that that was the actual time, hour, minute, when that bus was located there, when they captured that image, that is?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I would have to examine that image. I believe it says approximately 1400, that is 2.00 p.m. That's the way the image was provided to us by the U.S. government. And as to the timings of those images, I believe that's a matter for the U.S. government and the Rule 70 issues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, certainly I would suspect that you as an investigator, you must have asked how often, you know, you would get this imagery. Can they do it every second or is it every 10 seconds, every minute? How does it work in a general fashion. I'm not asking to go into any national secrets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is clearly in line of Rule 70 and the capabilities of this particular imagery, Your Honour. And if the exhibit that Mr. Manning has referred to is an exhibit in this case and has the time marked on it. And Mr. Karnavas can certainly ask questions about that exhibit. But as for -- I mean, we don't even know these sorts of questions. But it's clearly in the area of Rule 70 issue. What kind of capability the U.S. aerial imagery had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, if I may explain first, Your Honour. I'm not asking for them to divulge U.S. secrets, though probably this is not much of a U.S. secret. I'm merely asking whether the follow-up question would have been: Are you capable to provide us with an image, say, an hour later? Or a witness says that this incident happened around 6.00 in the afternoon, can you check your records and see whether there's an image on that particular hour to see if there's any changes so we have a before and after? That's what I'm getting at, Your Honour. Maybe I'm not phrasing my question correctly, maybe I'm not being articulate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you get the gist of what I'm asking, don't you, Mr. Manning?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, numerous requests were made for the best available material they could have given us under your rules and obligations. If they could have given me an image of men being executed and falling to the ground, I would have appreciated that from an investigative point of view. We gained the images that we were able to we gain from the U.S. government. I didn't make those initial requests. I have made requests of them and the U.S. government provided what they were able to or allowed to provide; they are the images we have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, gratuitous comments are not very helpful here as I am beginning to find out after several months in trial. So I didn't ask you whether -- that you could find images of people being shot and falling down. All right? I'm asking whether you made a request or whether you know a I know you a request was made. I know that you made many requests. But concretely, can you tell me: Was a request made once they came up with this photograph of -- where there is a bus, did you make a request and say we have a window of opportunity here where witnesses are saying that an incident happened three hours or four hours or five hours later, could you check your records and see if there is an image so we can see whether there is any difference, you know, in the pictures. That's all I'm asking. Was a specific request made now that you've had some indicators as to the timing of certain events from witnesses. And as you know, sometimes witnesses are not totally accurate on the timing under stressful circumstances.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I didn't make, in that instance, those requests. Numerous requests were made. If we received a photograph like that, we would request the next best photo or the next image or the next time. We got what we got from the U.S. government. I didn't make those specific requests.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Thank you for answer my question. Now, Mr. Manning, I've looked at these photographs, and like you, I've spent a lifetime basically in this forensic area and I haven't been able to make sense of some of these photographs. Perhaps I don't have a trained eye. Did you have that sort of trained eye to look at the photographs, or did you need some assistance from the U.S. government or their specialists who would be able to look at a photograph and be able to say, okay this looks like --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I haven't finished my question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That this is an excavator or this is a bus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: That is an overbroad question. I don't know if Mr. Karnavas is referring to a particular photograph. Perhaps he can be more specific. I don't see how --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I gave an example, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I don't know how this witness can answer this question when it's put that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, you may concentrate your answer on this photograph, whether it's a bus or an excavator.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. I just happened to be the Rule 70 person of the team, and I have no objection to that particular question as you've phrased it. The question about any particular dealings or communications he's had with any United States aerial imagery analysts is a question that is not appropriate and is off-limits. And it's a very serious issue in that how this material is dealt with in this court will determine in the future how governments work with future tribunals. So it's a very serious situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Your Honour, I'm not asking him to interpret photos from the Cuban missile crisis. I'm asking him whether with his trained eye he could identify him or did he need assistance. I don't need the methodology that was used, just whether he needed assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Witness, you may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the instance where a bus is sighted outside the Kravica warehouse, I can clearly see that's a bus. I need no assistance in saying that. A similar instance at the Sandici meadow where there is four or five or more buses and clearly trucks and vehicles. I can clearly see those. Some images are not the best quality. I can clearly see the majority of the things indicated on those photographs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, were you able to see them or identify them, as you say, clearly, with the naked eye, or did you need to have those photographs blown up in order to -- or maybe in between you used a magnifying glass. I'm talking about what you did and I'm not talking about the U.S. government. I know they have their own sophisticated methods.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, going back to the bus at the Kravica warehouse, it's -- that I've seen an A4 photograph, it's clear to the naked eye. I have examined a lot of those photographs with a magnifying glass, but to me with the naked eye, that's clearly a bus and that's clearly the warehouse. But there are other photographs which are not as good of quality. If you saw some of them, particularly some of the Zeleni Jadar secondary photographs, some are good and some are bad. In those instances, in those examples, I could see what I know to be a bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the answer to my question was: You didn't need to blow up any of these photographs?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Prior to this mission here in part of your work, because I understand you have a long history of law enforcement, did you work with aerial imagery before where you had to discern what was on these photographs -- on photographs?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: On a limited occasions. When I was in the drug operations' branch, we would use helicopters or fixed-wing overflights of plantations. We would use it on occasion for identifying premises, and normal aerial photography.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are there forensic experts? Again, I'm not asking you about the official U.S. government experts, but are there forensic experts that have as a specialty the interpretation of photographs such as this, the ones that we're dealing with, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, there are photographic imagery experts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And may I ask if any were consulted since it would appear that there seemed to be no shortage of forensic experts or fields of expertise engaged in this case in order to be as precise as possible?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honour, not to my knowledge, but I'm not going to deal with the U.S. aerial imagery and how that was processed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about the U.S. imagery. Okay. I'm just asking: Did you want a second opinion, for instance, from an expert, I mean such as with the ballistics, for instance, we can look with the naked eye or put it under a comparison microscope and see two casings and to see whether there is the ejection marks. I understand that. And maybe you can reach the same conclusion. But nonetheless, you went to an expert so the expert could then produce a report which we would have a little more reliability. In this case, even though with your untrained eye, so to speak, you were able to identify what you think was a bus. My question is: Did you go to an expert, then, a forensic expert, specialising in this to verify what you believe was the correct answer in this photograph?
